questions.question: On a shoreline cleanup at Spanish Banks, Jae's group fills one bag with 10 pieces of litter: 4 plastic straws and 6 bottle caps. Jae wants to report the part of all the litter in the bag that was straws. Which representation shows that?
options: The fraction 4/10
The ratio 4:6
The fraction 4/6
The fraction 6/10
questions.explain: A part-to-whole representation compares the part with the total: 4 straws out of 10 pieces is 4/10. The common trap is 4:6, which compares straws with caps (part to part) instead of with the whole bag.

questions.question: A Grade 7 class surveys 50 students about hot lunch. Exactly 30 students choose pizza and the other 20 choose noodles. The newsletter wants the pizza result written as a percent of all the students surveyed. Which percent is correct?
questions.explain: Compare the part with the whole group: 30 out of 50 is 30/50 = 60/100 = 60%. The trap is comparing the 30 pizza votes with the 20 noodle votes (30:20 = 150%), which is part-to-part and is not a percent of the class.

questions.question: A hoodie at a Kelowna shop costs $40. The sign says 25% off. Which expression represents the amount of money Sam saves?
questions.explain: Percent off means the discount is that percent of the original price: 0.25 × $40 = $10 saved. The trap is 0.75 × $40 = $30, which is the sale price you pay, not the amount saved.

questions.question: A shoreline cleanup has 3 equal groups. Exactly 2 of the 3 groups finish their section early. Ana must record the part of all the groups that finished early on a chart, and the value must be exact (not rounded). Which representation should she use?
options: The ratio 2:1
The decimal 0.67
The decimal 0.6
The fraction 2/3, because 2 ÷ 3 = 0.666... is a repeating decimal
questions.explain: 2 ÷ 3 gives the repeating decimal 0.666..., so only the fraction 2/3 records it exactly; 0.67 and 0.6 are rounded. The trap is 2:1, which compares the groups that finished with the one that did not, not with all 3 groups.

questions.question: Class A has 25 students and 18 of them want the ski trip. In Class B, 70% of the students want the ski trip. Which is the best way to decide which class wants the trip more?
options: Write 18/25 as a percent: 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, which is greater than 70%.
Write Class A as 18:7, about 257%, and compare that with 70%.
Compare 18 with 70; 70 is greater, so Class B wants it more.
Compare the numerators of 18/25 and 70/100; 70 is greater, so Class B.
questions.explain: Percents put both classes on the same whole of 100, so change 18/25 to 72% and compare with 70%. The trap is 18:7, which compares the yes votes with the no votes and can never be compared with a percent of the class.

questions.question: The same jacket costs $60 at two stores. Store A advertises 20% off. Store B advertises $15 off. Which reasoning correctly decides where the jacket is cheaper?
options: 20% off a $60 jacket means the sale price is $12, so Store A is cheaper.
0.20 × $60 = $12 off at Store A, which is less than $15 off, so Store B is cheaper.
Compare 20 and 15; 20 is greater, so Store A takes more off.
The $15 off is 15% of $60, which is less than 20%, so Store A takes more off.
questions.explain: To compare a percent with a dollar amount, write both in the same form: 0.20 × $60 = $12 off versus $15 off, so Store B ($45) beats Store A ($48). The trap is reading the $12 as the price you pay instead of the amount taken off.

questions.question: Kai is typing survey results into a spreadsheet and each cell must hold an exact decimal. Which result cannot be written as an exact terminating decimal, so the fraction is the better representation to keep?
questions.explain: 2 ÷ 9 = 0.222..., a repeating decimal, so only the fraction keeps it exact; 7/8 = 0.875, 3/5 = 0.6 and 1/4 = 0.25 all terminate. The trap is assuming every fraction turns into a short decimal that ends.

questions.question: In a travel survey of one Grade 7 class, 12 students bike to school and 18 students walk. No one else was surveyed. The poster must show the part of the students surveyed who bike, written as a percent. Which percent is correct?
questions.explain: The whole is all 30 students surveyed, so bikers are 12/30 = 4/10 = 40%. The trap is 12/18, about 66.7%, which compares bikers with walkers (part to part) rather than with the whole group.

questions.question: A board game is $45 and the store sign says 30% off. Maya works out 0.30 × $45 = $13.50. Which statement about her $13.50 is correct?
options: 30% off means $30 off the price, so Maya pays $45 − $30 = $15.
The discount is $31.50, so Maya pays $13.50, the 30% she worked out.
The $13.50 is the discount, so Maya pays $45 − $13.50 = $31.50.
The $13.50 is the sale price, so Maya pays $13.50 and saves $31.50.
questions.explain: Taking a percent of the price gives the amount taken off, so $13.50 is the discount and the price paid is $45 − $13.50 = $31.50. The trap is treating the discount as if it were the new price.

questions.question: Two cleanup groups sort their litter. Group A collects 40 items and 24 of them are plastic. Group B collects 45 items and 27 of them are plastic. Which group had the greater part of its litter as plastic?
options: Group B, because 27 plastic items is more than 24 plastic items.
Both groups are the same: 24/40 = 60% and 27/45 = 60%.
Group A, because 24:16 simplifies to 3:2, so 3/2 of Group A's litter was plastic.
They cannot be compared, because the groups collected different total numbers of items.
questions.explain: Percents give both groups the same whole: 24/40 = 60% and 27/45 = 60%, so the plastic rates are equal even though the totals differ. Two traps hide here: comparing raw counts, and using 24:16, which compares plastic with non-plastic and so can never be the part of the whole.

questions.question: A Grade 7 class of 60 students votes for a class pet. The results come in three different forms: fish were chosen by 1/4 of the class, dogs by 0.35 of the class, and the ratio of cat votes to non-cat votes is 3:7. Which pet was most popular, and why?
options: Cats — the ratio 3:7 means 3/7, about 43%, which beats fish at 25% and dogs at 35%.
Fish — 1/4 written as a decimal is 0.4, which is more than 0.35 for dogs or 0.3 for cats.
Dogs — change every result to a percent of the class: fish 25%, dogs 35%, cats 30%.
Rabbits — the students left over after fish, dogs and cats must form the biggest group of all.
questions.explain: Rewrite all three forms as percents of the same whole: fish 25%, dogs 35%, and cats 3:7 means 3 out of every 10 students, or 30%, so dogs win. The trap is reading 3:7 as 3/7 — that ratio compares cats with non-cats, so the whole is 3 + 7 = 10.

questions.question: A pair of runners costs $80 at both stores. Store A advertises 1/4 off. Store B advertises 20% off, and then a $5 coupon comes off the already reduced price. Which reasoning finds the cheaper store?
options: 1/4 off a $80 pair means you pay 1/4 of $80, which is $20, and Store B cannot beat a $20 price, so Store A is cheaper by far.
1/4 = 25% and 25% is more than 20%, so Store A always saves more; the small $5 coupon cannot change which percent is bigger.
20% of $80 is $16, and then the coupon takes another $5 off that, so at Store B you pay $16 − $5 = $11, which is cheapest.
In dollars off, Store A takes off $20 while Store B takes off $16 and then $5, that is $21, so Store B costs less ($59 vs $60).
questions.explain: Put both offers in the same representation — dollars off: 1/4 × $80 = $20 off ($60 to pay), while 0.20 × $80 = $16 off plus the $5 coupon is $21 off ($59 to pay). The trap is treating the amount taken off as the price you pay, or comparing 25% with 20% while ignoring the extra $5.
